report:
::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"}

Power analyses need to contain the following information to be interpretable: the type of power analysis, the statistical test, the software used, sample size, critical alpha criterion, power level, effect size, and an effect size metric. In addition, it is recommended to make sure the power analysis is reproducible (by sharing the code, or a screenshot, of the power analysis), and to provide good arguments for why the study was designed to detect an effect of this size.

For an a-priori power analysis, where the sample size is determined, reporting all information would look like:

> An a priori power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that for a Cohen's d = 0.5, an alpha level of 0.05, and a desired power level of 80% required at least 64 participants in each group.

For a sensitivity power analysis, this sentence would look like:

> A sensitivity power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that with 64 participants in each group, and an alpha level of 0.05, a desired power level of 80% was reached for an effect size of d = 0.5.

info.title: Translational Neuroscience in Psychoeducation: Mapping Non-Motor Circuitry to Clinical Management in Movement Disorders

text.text: Non-motor symptoms (NMS) affect nearly all patients with Parkinson's disease (PD) and related movement disorders, with a mean of roughly 8 to 10 discrete symptoms per individual.

Their effect on quality of life often exceeds that of motor features, yet NMS remain under-recognized and undertreated, partly because patients and caregivers lack a working model of why these symptoms arise in a "movement" disease.
This chapter applies neuroscience-informed psychoeducation (NIPE) to that gap and positions it relative to conventional psychoeducation, health communication, and behavioral science.
We propose the Map-Normalize-Differentiate-Navigate (MNDN) workflow as a movement-disordersspecific implementation of the NIPE framework described in Chapter 1 of this volume.
MNDN is a clinical proposal, not a validated protocol: its components are specified so that it can be tested, but its effects on patient outcomes have not been evaluated.

Drawing on the tripartite cortico-basal gangliathalamocortical loop model and multi-transmitter degeneration, we provide modules for seven high-yield NMS: apathy, anxiety, executive dysfunction, REM sleep behavior disorder, neurogenic orthostatic hypotension, psychosis, and fatigue.

Each module summarizes the neural systems implicated, at the level of certainty the evidence supports, together with common misattributions, reversible contributors that must be excluded, management options and their limits, and patient and caregiver handout content.

We describe delivery formats from 3-5 minute "micro-NIPE" sessions in routine visits to group and telehealth programs, specify the minimum components, provider competencies, dose, fidelity criteria, and proximal outcomes needed to test MNDN, and examine the ethical risks of neurobiological framing (determinism, oversimplification, over-attribution, and false reassurance), with particular attention to prognostic counseling in REM sleep behavior disorder.
NIPE in movement disorders is designed to reduce self-blame, support accurate symptom attribution, and improve collaborative management.
Whether it does so is an empirical question that this chapter aims to make answerable.
>CLINICAL RATIONALE AND LEARNING OBJECTIVES

text.text: Movement disorders, Parkinson's disease (PD) foremost among them, are conventionally taught as motor syndromes.

Yet nearly all patients report at least one non-motor symptom (NMS; 98.6% in the PRIAMO study), with a mean of roughly 8 to 10 discrete NMS per individual. 1, 2 Depression, anxiety, apathy, cognitive impairment, sleep disturbance, autonomic dysfunction, fatigue, and psychosis often affect quality of life more than the motor features that dominate the clinical encounter.

text.text: NMS nonetheless remain under-recognized and undertreated. 2 We suggest two reasons: patients and caregivers have no working model of why these symptoms appear in a "movement" disease, and clinicians lack a structured way to explain them in the time a visit allows.

text.text: Neuroscience-informed psychoeducation (NIPE) offers one response to this gap.

As defined in Chapter 1 of this volume, NIPE differs from conventional psychoeducation on two dimensions: content that centers on brain-based explanations of symptoms, treatment response, and recovery, and a delivery structure designed around how the brain learns. 3, 4 This chapter adapts NIPE to movement disorders and proposes the Map-Normalize-Differentiate-Navigate (MNDN) workflow as a movement-disorders-specific implementation of that framework rather than a separate model.

text.text: MNDN is presented as a clinical proposal whose components are specified well enough to be tested (Section 6.2); its effects on patient outcomes have not been evaluated.
The workflow is intended for neurologists, advanced practice providers, psychologists, nurses, and social workers, in formats from brief bedside sessions to group telehealth programs.
Psychoeducation has a substantial evidence base outside neurology.

In schizophrenia, structured programs combining illness information, skills training, problem-solving, and family involvement reduce relapse and rehospitalization and improve adherence, and psychoeducation is classed as an evidence-based practice in its own right. 5, 6 Its active ingredients are usually described as information transfer, emotional processing, skill acquisition, and support, delivered within a collaborative relationship rather than as a lecture. 5 Psychoeducation programs for PD patients and carers follow the same pattern and have been implemented and evaluated in primary care; in the completed controlled evaluation, psychoeducation and education arms both improved, with no between-group difference. 7, 8 Behavioral science explains why information changes behavior only under particular conditions, and each condition maps onto a step of MNDN.

text.text: Structure: content is selected and delivered to be salient, trustworthy, dosed to avoid overload, repeated, motivating, multimodal, and interactive.

Mechanism: brain-based framing is proposed to work by improving mechanism-informed self-awareness, reappraising the emotional meaning of a symptom (from personal failing to circuit dysfunction), reducing internalized stigma, and supporting agency through explicit links between understanding and action.

Chapter 1 also sets the boundary condition that governs this chapter: NIPE operates within the biopsychosocial model and is not a reductionist alternative to it. 3, 16 The most tested precedent in a neurological population is pain neuroscience education, in which reconceptualizing chronic pain as a nervous-system phenomenon rather than tissue damage produces modest but consistent reductions in pain, disability, and catastrophizing when combined with active treatment. 17, 18 That literature also shows the limits: education alone rarely changes outcomes, effects depend on delivery quality, and brain-based framing carries risks of its own.

>NON-MOTOR SYMPTOM BURDEN AND MEASUREMENT-BASED CARE
text.formatted: <head n="2." >NON-MOTOR SYMPTOM BURDEN AND MEASUREMENT-BASED CARE</head>

text.text: The range of NMS in PD is wide.

A large clinic-based cohort study using the MDS-UPDRS Part I identifies cognitive impairment (74.3%), nighttime sleep problems (71.6%), urinary dysfunction (71.6%), fatigue (68.7%), pain (64.2%), daytime somnolence (61.9%), and depressed mood (60.8%) as the most frequently reported NMS. 23 Hallucinations (13.8%) and impulse control disorders (7.7%) are less common early in the disease but carry disproportionate clinical weight.

text.text: NMS burden increases with disease duration, cognitive impairment, levodopa dose, and the postural instability/gait disorder (PIGD) motor subtype. 23 Gastrointestinal dysfunction, neuropsychiatric disturbances, and sleep disorders may predate motor onset by years, which is one reason PD is now regarded as a multisystem synucleinopathy from its inception. 24 As a group, NMS affect health-related quality of life more than motor severity does. 25

>TRANSLATIONAL CIRCUIT ATLAS FOR NON-MOTOR SYMPTOMS
text.formatted: <head n="3." >TRANSLATIONAL CIRCUIT ATLAS FOR NON-MOTOR SYMPTOMS</head>

text.text: The classical Alexander/DeLong model describes three functionally segregated, parallel cortico-basal ganglia-thalamocortical (CBGTC) loops: 30, 31 1.
text.formatted: The classical Alexander/DeLong model describes three functionally segregated, parallel cortico-basal ganglia-thalamocortical (CBGTC) loops: <ref type="bibr" target="#b29">30,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b30">31</ref> 1.

text.text: Motor loop: Supplementary motor area (SMA) ↔ putamen ↔ globus pallidus internus/substantia nigra pars reticulata (GPi/SNr) ↔ ventrolateral (VL) thalamus → SMA.
This loop governs voluntary movement and is the primary target of levodopa therapy and deep brain stimulation.
GPi/SNr ↔ ventral anterior/mediodorsal (VA/MD) thalamus → DLPFC.
This loop supports working memory, cognitive flexibility, planning, and set-shifting. 31 3.
text.formatted: This loop supports working memory, cognitive flexibility, planning, and set-shifting. <ref type="bibr" target="#b30">31</ref> 3.

text.text: Limbic loop: Orbitofrontal cortex (OFC) and anterior cingulate cortex (ACC) ↔ ventral striatum (nucleus accumbens) ↔ ventral pallidum/medial SNr ↔ MD thalamus → OFC/ACC.

This loop processes reward valuation, motivation, emotional regulation, and social cognition. 30 Although traditionally drawn as closed and parallel, later work describes cross-talk between loops, including a ventral striatum to medial substantia nigra to motor thalamus route through which limbic activity can influence motor output, demonstrated by tract-tracing and circuit manipulation in animals. 32, 33 This open pathway offers a plausible, though not established in humans, substrate for clinical observations such as worse motor performance during severe apathy or tremor amplification under anxiety.

text.text: In PD, dopamine loss follows a characteristic dorsal-to-ventral gradient within the striatum: the putamen is depleted earliest and most severely, followed by the dorsal caudate, and finally the ventral striatum.

One proposed staging model (PDFCD) maps this gradient onto a sequence of cognitive-behavioral change: executive dysfunction and mental fatigue first (Stage I; DLPFC-dorsal caudate), then depression and anxiety (Stage IIa; OFC-ventral caudate) and apathy (Stage IIb; ACC-nucleus accumbens), with dementia (Stage III) when cortical dopamine projections themselves degenerate. 34 The sequence describes group tendencies.

text.text: Individual patients depart from it, and cholinergic, serotonergic, and noradrenergic loss, cortical Lewy pathology, medication, and comorbidity alter the picture at every stage.

Although dopamine loss dominates the PD narrative, NMS have been linked to degeneration across several neurotransmitter systems: • Serotonin (raphe nuclei): associated with depression, fatigue, and PD psychosis (5-HT₂A receptor upregulation is one proposed mechanism) [35] [36] [37] • Norepinephrine (locus coeruleus): associated with anxiety, autonomic failure, and attentional dysfunction 38, 39 • Acetylcholine (nucleus basalis of Meynert, pedunculopontine nucleus): associated with cognitive decline, hallucinations, and REM sleep behavior disorder 40 • GABA/glycine (brainstem reticular formation): implicated in REM sleep behavior disorder through failure of REM atonia circuits 41 Explaining this multi-transmitter reality to patients is foundational to NIPE: it normalizes NMS ("these symptoms come from the same disease process") and explains why motor medications alone may not resolve every complaint.

text.text: Two caveats govern how the atlas is used in this chapter.
First, its associations are population-level: an imaging difference between apathetic and non-apathetic groups does not establish the mechanism in a given patient.

Second, most NMS are multiply determined, by disease stage, medication state, sleep, mood, comorbid illness, psychological adjustment, and social circumstance, in proportions that differ between patients.
The atlas is therefore used to generate candidate explanations that the Differentiate step tests, not to assign each symptom to a circuit.
>THE NIPE FRAMEWORK AND MAP-NORMALIZE-DIFFERENTIATE-NAVIGATE WORKFLOW (MNDN)
text.formatted: <head n="4." >THE NIPE FRAMEWORK AND MAP-NORMALIZE-DIFFERENTIATE-NAVIGATE WORKFLOW (MNDN)</head>

text.text: Chapter 1 characterizes a NIPE intervention by its content (neuroscience factual information, brain strategies, and brain activities), its structure (salience, trustworthiness, intensity or dose, repetition, motivation, multimedia delivery, and interaction), and its delivery within a person-centered therapeutic context with attention to timing and readiness.

3,4 MNDN adds nothing to this framework; it sequences its elements for a movement-disorders clinic, where NMS compete with motor assessment for a 20-minute visit and where the differential diagnosis of any NMS includes medication effects and fluctuations peculiar to dopaminergic therapy.

Content is organized by Research Domain Criteria (RDoC) domains: negative valence (anxiety), positive valence (reward, motivation), cognitive systems (executive function), arousal and regulatory systems (sleep, fatigue, autonomic function), and social processes.

text.text: Each step below states its purpose, a sample script, and the error it is designed to prevent.
Step 2 -NORMALIZE Purpose: remove blame.

Normalization has two targets, the experience (common, recognized, not a character flaw) and the attribution (a symptom of the illness rather than of the person): "Roughly four in ten people with Parkinson's have this.
It is not laziness and it is not giving up."
Normalizing the experience does not require asserting that this patient's symptom is disease-intrinsic; that question stays open until Step 3.
Reduced self-blame and caregiver frustration are the proximal targets. 43, 44 The error prevented is moral attribution by the patient or family.
text.formatted: Reduced self-blame and caregiver frustration are the proximal targets. <ref type="bibr" target="#b42">43,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b43">44</ref> The error prevented is moral attribution by the patient or family.

text.text: Purpose: test the population-level association against the individual.
The clinician names the alternatives aloud, because doing so is itself psychoeducation: it shows the patient that "Parkinson's" is a hypothesis rather than a verdict.

Alternatives fall into five groups: medication effects (impulse control disorder from dopamine agonists, sedation from anticholinergics or benzodiazepines, wearing-off), comorbid medical conditions (hypothyroidism, anemia, sleep apnea, B12 deficiency), psychiatric comorbidity (a preexisting anxiety or depressive disorder), psychological and social contributors (grief over the diagnosis, role loss, caregiver strain, financial pressure), and reversible precipitants (infection, dehydration, sleep loss).
The step ends with a stated working formulation and, where indicated, tests.
The error prevented is over-attribution, in which every new symptom is assigned to PD.
Purpose: convert the formulation into a plan the patient has chosen.

Using elicit-provide-elicit, the clinician asks what the patient already knows or wants, provides options with their mechanism and limits, and elicits a response before agreeing on a first step: "Given what we have discussed, what feels like the most important first step to you?"
14, 15 The plan may include medication adjustment, behavioral strategies, referral, and a defined follow-up at which the explanation is revisited and revised if the response is not as expected.

text.text: An explanation that cannot be revised is the deterministic framing this chapter tries to avoid.
The error prevented is a plan the patient did not choose and will not follow.
Metaphors appear only in the patient-facing handouts, at most one per module, introduced as a simplification ("one way to picture this").
The clinician-facing Circuit Explanation in each module states the scientific account separately so that teaching device and evidence are not conflated.

Metaphors are memorable, but they also shape inference: an amygdala "alarm" implies a single locus for anxiety, which the evidence does not support, and a "CEO" prefrontal cortex implies a hierarchy the anatomy does not show. 45, 46 The handouts retain two labeled metaphors (an alarm system that is easier to set off, for anxiety; a brake on movement during dreams that no longer holds, for RBD) and drop the rest.

Apathy in PD has been associated most consistently with dysfunction of the mesocorticolimbic dopamine system (ventral tegmental area to nucleus accumbens, anterior cingulate, and orbitofrontal cortex), with additional serotonergic involvement.
In this model the ACC-accumbens link integrates effort cost with expected reward; when its dopaminergic modulation falls, patients find it harder to mobilize effort toward goals they still value.

Imaging studies report ventral striatal and ACC gray-matter loss and blunted reward sensitivity (for example, reduced pupillary dilation to incentive cues) in apathetic compared with nonapathetic patients, and dopaminergic medication partly restores reward sensitivity in the ON state without abolishing the deficit. [47] [48] [49] [50] These are group-level differences.

text.text: Apathy is heterogeneous: it overlaps with depression and cognitive impairment, varies with dopaminergic state, can appear after abrupt dopaminergic reduction (for example after subthalamic DBS), and is shaped by mood, cognition, and the social environment.

The circuit account explains part of the variance, not all of it. 44, 47 • Depression (overlapping but distinct; apathy lacks the sadness and guilt of depression) • Laziness or "giving up" (a moral judgment that increases caregiver resentment) • Medication oversedation • Depression (screen with PHQ-9) • Hypothyroidism (TSH) • Medication-induced sedation (review anticholinergics, benzodiazepines) • Dopaminergic under-replacement or recent dose reduction, including after DBS • Demoralization (a reactive psychological state responsive to counseling) • Optimize dopaminergic therapy; dopamine agonists with D₃ affinity may improve apathy in some patients, at the cost of impulse control disorder risk 51 • Rivastigmine has modest trial evidence 51 • Behavioral activation (structured daily activity schedules) and goal-setting with caregiver support are low-risk first-line approaches • No pharmacologic treatment is FDA-approved specifically for PD apathy; clinicians should communicate this uncertainty to patients 51, 52

text.text: What is apathy in Parkinson's?
Apathy means reduced motivation: less interest in activities, less initiative, less emotional engagement.
It is not laziness.
It is linked to changes in the brain's reward and motivation circuit, the system that helps you start and finish things.
Your doctor will also check for other causes, such as depression, thyroid problems, or medication effects, because these can look similar and are treatable.
What can help?
• Structured daily schedules with specific, achievable goals • Caregiver support through gentle cueing (not nagging) and recognizing small completions
For caregivers: Apathy is not personal rejection.
It reflects a change in a brain circuit.
Gentle encouragement and breaking tasks into smaller steps can help.

Anxiety in PD has been associated with structural and functional changes in two overlapping systems: the threat-processing network (amygdala, anterior cingulate, medial prefrontal cortex, insula, hippocampus, striatum) and the limbic CBGTC loop.

Reported findings include reduced amygdala and ACC gray-matter volume, altered amygdala-orbitofrontal and amygdala-hippocampal connectivity, correlations between anxiety severity and reduced dopamine transporter binding in caudate, putamen, and thalamus and reduced norepinephrine transporter availability in caudate, thalamus, and amygdala, and white-matter changes in striato-orbitofrontal and striato-cingulate tracts. 38, 53, 54 Most of these are cross-sectional associations in modest samples, and they coexist with contributors that no circuit explains: adjustment to the diagnosis, fear of falling, embarrassment about visible symptoms, financial and role change, and preexisting anxiety disorders, which are common. 55, 56 The strongest disease-specific signal is temporal.

Autonomic mimics are critically important: • Wearing-off-related non-motor fluctuations can produce panic-like episodes (sweating, palpitations, inner restlessness) that wax and wane with dopaminergic medication cycles • Orthostatic hypotension may produce lightheadedness misinterpreted as anxiety • Akathisia from dopamine-receptor blocking agents • Hyperthyroidism, stimulant or caffeine excess, and cardiac causes of palpitations • Pre-existing anxiety disorders may coexist and compound 57 • SSRIs/SNRIs are first-line for persistent anxiety, with attention to potential tremor worsening (rare) or restless legs syndrome exacerbation • CBT adapted for PD has emerging support • Benzodiazepines should generally be avoided because of fall risk and cognitive effects • Optimization of dopaminergic therapy to reduce OFF-state anxiety is underused 58 Patient/Caregiver Handout -Anxiety Module Why does anxiety happen in Parkinson's?
Parkinson's changes several chemical messengers (dopamine, norepinephrine, and serotonin) that help regulate the brain's response to threat.
One way to picture this: the brain's alarm system becomes easier to set off.
This is a simplification.
Anxiety also comes from the real stresses of living with Parkinson's, and both deserve attention.
Watch for medication-related mimics: Some anxiety-like symptoms (racing heart, sweating, restlessness) may signal that your Parkinson's medication is wearing off.
Keep a diary of when symptoms occur relative to medication doses.
What can help?

• Breathing exercises and mindfulness techniques • Regular physical activity • Medication timing adjustment • Counseling or cognitive behavioral therapy Red flags, seek urgent care: Suicidal thoughts, panic attacks with chest pain, sudden inability to function.
Executive functions (working memory, cognitive flexibility, planning, response inhibition) depend on the associative loop linking DLPFC, dorsal caudate, GPi/SNr, and VA/MD thalamus.

Dopamine loss in the dorsal caudate is thought to reduce dopaminergic modulation of this loop, sometimes described as functional deafferentation of prefrontal cortex, and this is the leading explanation for the early difficulty with set-shifting (the neurological counterpart of "cognitive rigidity"), multitasking, and planning that roughly 30% of patients show; these deficits are associated with later dementia risk. 31, 34, 59 Other systems contribute and become dominant with progression: cholinergic loss from the nucleus basalis, cortical Lewy and amyloid pathology, and noradrenergic loss affecting attention.

text.text: What is executive dysfunction?
The front part of the brain (the prefrontal cortex) plans, organizes, and switches between tasks.
In Parkinson's, the chemical link between this region and a deeper structure called the caudate nucleus weakens, so multitasking, problem-solving, and changing plans take more effort.
Sleep problems, low mood, and some medicines can make this worse, and those can be treated.
• Use written schedules and checklists
REM sleep behavior disorder (RBD) arises from loss of the brainstem circuit that produces REM atonia.

Glutamatergic neurons of the sublaterodorsal tegmental nucleus (SLD, subcoeruleus) excite GABA/glycinergic neurons in the ventral medulla and spinal cord that inhibit motor neurons during REM sleep; alpha-synuclein pathology and loss of specific neuronal populations (including Crhbp-expressing neurons) in the SLD have been documented in PD patients with RBD, and lesions of these nuclei reproduce the phenotype in animals. 41, 61 This is among the better-established circuit accounts in this chapter.

62,66,67 Patient/Caregiver Handout -RBD and Sleep Module What is RBD?
During normal dreaming sleep, the brain holds the body still so that dreams are not acted out.
In RBD, the brainstem circuit that does this is affected by the same protein changes seen in Parkinson's.
One way to picture this: a brake on movement during dreams no longer holds.
The result is movement during dreams, sometimes kicking, punching, or falling out of bed.

Safety first: • Remove sharp objects from the bedroom • Place padding on bedside furniture • Consider bed rails • Sleep separately if injury risk is high Treatment options: Melatonin (taken at bedtime) is usually tried first.
If it is not enough, a low-dose sedative (clonazepam) may be recommended, with monitoring for daytime drowsiness.
About the future: RBD can occur on its own, and for some people it is an early sign of Parkinson's or a related condition.
Not everyone with RBD develops these conditions, and no test can say when or whether it will happen for one person.
Regular follow-up with a neurologist allows monitoring, early treatment if changes appear, and a conversation about research studies if you are interested.
Ask as many or as few questions about the future as you want; your doctor will follow your lead.

Neurogenic orthostatic hypotension (nOH) in PD results from alpha-synuclein-mediated degeneration of peripheral sympathetic (postganglionic noradrenergic) neurons and, to a variable and less wellcharacterized extent, central autonomic pathways.

Cardiac sympathetic denervation is a hallmark of PD and distinguishes it from MSA, where preganglionic loss predominates. 68 The result is failure to release norepinephrine on standing, inadequate vasoconstriction, and a fall of ≥20 mmHg in systolic or ≥10 mmHg in diastolic blood pressure within 3 minutes of standing. 69, 70 The peripheral mechanism is well established; in practice, medication contributions are so common that nOH is best regarded as intrinsic denervation plus whatever the drug list adds.

text.text: What is neurogenic orthostatic hypotension?
When you stand up, your body normally tightens blood vessels to keep blood flowing to your brain.
In Parkinson's, the nerves that control this reflex can be damaged, causing a blood pressure drop when standing.
This leads to lightheadedness, dizziness, or fainting.
Some medicines add to the problem, so your doctor will review your full list.
Practical strategies:

Rise slowly from lying or sitting positions • Drink adequate fluids • Consider increased salt intake (discuss with your physician) • Wear compression stockings or abdominal binders • Avoid standing still for prolonged periods • Eat smaller, more frequent meals Medications: Droxidopa or midodrine may be prescribed.
Take them in the morning and afternoon, not at bedtime, to avoid high blood pressure while lying down.
PD psychosis (PDP), which encompasses visual hallucinations, illusions, sense of presence, paranoid ideation, and delusions, has several partly overlapping explanatory models rather than one.

The most influential pharmacological model treats it as a serotonin-dopamine imbalance: cortical Lewy pathology is proposed to drive compensatory upregulation of 5-HT₂A receptors in temporal and ventral visual cortex, and excessive 5-HT₂A signaling is hypothesized to generate visual hallucinations and, through enhanced ventral striatal dopamine activity, delusions.

The model draws support from the 5-HT₂A agonism of serotonergic psychedelics and from the efficacy of the 5-HT₂A inverse agonist pimavanserin. 35, 37, 71 Other models emphasize cholinergic deficit (hallucinations improve with cholinesterase inhibitors and worsen with anticholinergics), impaired bottom-up visual processing with over-reliance on top-down expectation, attentional network dysfunction, and intrusion of REM phenomena into wakefulness. 40, 72 Dopaminergic medication lowers the threshold, but psychosis also occurs at low medication exposure, and cognitive impairment, visual loss, sleep disturbance, and age are independent risk factors.

What is Parkinson's psychosis?
Some people with Parkinson's see things that are not there (often people, animals, or shadows) or develop false beliefs (suspicion, paranoia).
This is not "madness."

It is linked to changes in several brain chemical systems, including serotonin receptors in the brain's visual areas, and it is often triggered or worsened by infections, dehydration, poor sleep, or medications.

text.text: What is Parkinson's fatigue?
Fatigue in Parkinson's is a persistent, overwhelming tiredness that is out of proportion to physical effort and is not relieved by rest.
It is a real symptom of the disease, linked to changes in several brain chemical systems, and it is not a sign of being out of shape or lazy.
Because sleep problems, low thyroid, anemia, depression, and some medicines can cause the same feeling, your doctor will check for these; several are treatable.
What can help?
• Regular exercise (aerobic and resistance training) • Good sleep habits • Treatment of depression or apathy if present • Pacing activities and planning rest periods
When to raise a concern: Fatigue that worsens suddenly, interferes with safety (drowsy driving), or comes with new symptoms.

text.text: The most scalable delivery model is the 3-5 minute "micro-NIPE" embedded in a routine clinic encounter.

After reviewing NMS screening scores, the clinician selects one symptom module, by the patient's priority rather than the clinician's, and walks the patient through the MNDN workflow using a laminated reference card or tablet-based visual aid.
A printed handout is provided at checkout.
Over successive visits, modules accumulate and build the patient's and caregiver's understanding of NMS as manifestations of the disease and of the other factors that shape them.

Practical tips for micro-NIPE: • Prepare materials in advance (laminated circuit diagrams, pre-printed handouts) • Select one NMS per visit to avoid overwhelming the patient • Use the MNDN workflow as a structured guide, including at least two named alternatives in the Differentiate step • Close with teach-back: ask the patient to say in their own words what the symptom is linked to and what the first step is • Document the psychoeducation provided in the clinical note • Schedule follow-up to assess understanding and outcomes

MNDN is described here at the level of detail needed for replication and evaluation, following the TIDieR checklist for intervention description and the Medical Research Council framework for complex interventions. 79, 80 Table 4 lists the minimum components, provider competencies, dose, fidelity criteria, and outcomes.

text.text: Two design choices deserve comment.

Proximal outcomes are prioritized: an educational intervention should first be shown to change what it directly targets (attribution, self-blame, self-efficacy, caregiver understanding, engagement, shared decision-making) before it is expected to change symptom severity or quality of life, which depend on many other inputs.
Fidelity is defined behaviorally so that it can be rated from a recording or a structured note, consistent with NIH Behavior Change Consortium recommendations.
Where resources permit, group sessions (6-10 patients with or without caregivers; 60-90 minutes; 4-8 weekly sessions) allow deeper engagement.
Each session covers one NIPE module with didactic content, facilitated discussion, and brief self-assessment exercises.
Group formats provide peer support, normalize experiences, and enable shared problem-solving.

Dyadic sessions (patient plus primary caregiver) are particularly valuable for: • Caregiver scaffolding training (Module III) • Psychosis management education (Module VI) • Safety planning for RBD (Module IV)
Group psychoeducation programs such as ReNACE have been delivered to PD patients and carers in primary care and evaluated in a controlled design.

Caregivers act as co-therapists in most of the modules above, and Chapter 1 identifies caregiver engagement as one of the mechanisms through which NIPE is proposed to work. 3 Dedicated caregiver content should include: • Understanding the biological basis of NMS (reducing blame), and its limits (not every symptom is the disease) • Scaffolding techniques for executive dysfunction • Safety planning for RBD and psychosis • Recognition of caregiver burnout and depression

Every Map statement is paired with something modifiable.

text.text: Individual variability is stated as a fact, not offered as an apology.
NIPE should inform choice, not replace it.
All management decisions are collaborative.

Deterministic language ("this will get worse") is replaced by probabilistic language ("in some people this symptom changes over time; we will watch for it together"), and the patient's priorities set the first step.
Normalization addresses the person's experience and the legitimacy of the symptom; it does not settle the cause.
The message that best protects against over-attribution is that understanding the neuroscience helps clinician and patient generate and test explanations rather than assign each symptom to a circuit.

In practice, a symptom is not attributed to PD, in the conversation or in the note, until the module's differentials have been considered, and the attribution is recorded as a working formulation that later visits can overturn.
RBD is the module in which NIPE conveys future risk as well as mechanism, and the risk is large.
Four principles apply.
Ask first: assess what the patient wants to know, and how much, before disclosing.

Preferences vary, some patients want full numerical risk and others want monitoring without prognosis, and both positions are legitimate and can change over time. 66, 67 Distinguish what is known from what is not: cohort risk (about 6% per year, roughly three quarters over 12 years in sleep-center cohorts) is known; the individual's timing, phenotype, and whether conversion will occur in their lifetime are not, and community-detected RBD may carry lower risk than the cohorts suggest. 62 Say what can be done now: the symptom can be treated, the bedroom made safe, and motor, cognitive, autonomic, and olfactory function monitored so that treatment starts early if needed; observational and interventional studies are available for those who want to take part.

Programs must plan for technology-limited populations with telephone-based or in-person alternatives.

Distal outcomes: whether proximal changes translate into lower NMS burden, better quality of life, lower caregiver burden, or changed healthcare utilization, and through which mediators.
Harms: prognostic pessimism, anxiety after RBD disclosure, over-attribution rates, and clinician empathy, measured prospectively rather than assumed absent.

Mechanism: whether circuit-based education changes metacognitive accuracy (for example, apathy self-awareness, which may itself relate to ACC-accumbens connectivity) or interoceptive awareness, and whether these changes track response.

Extension to other movement disorders: dystonia (sensorimotor integration), Huntington's disease (caudate-predominant degeneration with prominent psychiatric NMS), functional movement disorder (where predictive-processing explanations are already used therapeutically), and tic disorders (habit-loop circuitry).

text.text: Several NMS lack approved treatments, and off-label strategies carry uncertain benefit.
NIPE complements pharmacologic and rehabilitative care and does not replace it.
Clinicians should say as much: "This symptom is linked to brain changes that we understand in part.
Several things help many people.
We will find out what helps you, and we will change the explanation if the course tells us to."
• Non-motor symptoms affect nearly all patients with PD and often cause more disability than motor features.
Systematic screening with validated instruments is essential.
• NIPE extends established psychoeducation with brain-based content and a delivery structure built around how people learn; MNDN is its movement-disorders implementation, not a separate model.
• The tripartite CBGTC loop model and the multi-transmitter framework provide a translational scaffold for explaining NMS.
Its associations are population-level and are stated with the certainty the evidence supports.
• The MNDN workflow delivers one symptom per visit in 3-5 minutes.
The Differentiate step is what keeps normalization from becoming over-attribution.
• Patient and caregiver handouts reinforce clinic teaching; they use at most one labeled metaphor per module, and the scientific account is stated separately.
• Implementation can begin with micro-NIPE and scale to group, dyadic, and telehealth formats.

Including them is expected to benefit both patients and caregivers, and this expectation should be tested.

• Neurobiological framing has known risks (determinism, oversimplification, over-attribution, false reassurance, and reduced clinician empathy); the design features of MNDN are chosen to address them.
• • Proximal outcome trials should precede claims about effects on symptom severity or quality of life.

Using a visual aid (a laminated diagram of the three loops and the brainstem and autonomic systems, or a tablet animation), the clinician states the association at the level the evidence supports: "Low motivation in Parkinson's is linked to changes in the brain'sreward and motivation circuit, which sits deeper than the movement circuit and depends on the same chemical, dopamine.
That is the most likely explanation, and we will check for others."
"Linked" rather than "caused" is deliberate.
The error this step prevents is the absence of any model, which leaves the patient with the default explanations of aging, weakness, or character.

Standard antipsychotics (haloperidol, olanzapine, risperidone) are dangerous in Parkinson's and should be avoided.
